result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_resistance_distance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate the resistance distance between two nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L24865-L24954){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_resistance_distance( source, target, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Resistance distance](/assets/graphs/algo-resistance-distance.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two focal nodes A and B on the sides of the frame connected by two parallel two-hop paths, one through node C above and one through node D below. Every edge is drawn as a zigzag resistor symbol to make the electrical analogy explicit. A small overlay in the center reports the resulting effective resistance R(A, B) = 1, obtained by combining the two series paths in parallel." width="100%"} The resistance distance (also called effective resistance) is the electrical resistance between two nodes if each edge is replaced by a 1-ohm resistor. It is a metric on graphs that satisfies the triangle inequality and provides insight into network connectivity and robustness. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Source node identifier (ID or label). [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Target node identifier (ID or label). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The resistance distance between the two nodes. Returns `0.0` if source equals target. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed (resistance distance is only defined for undirected graphs). [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If either source or target node doesn't exist in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Effective resistance treats the graph as an electrical network where every edge is a 1-ohm resistor and reports the voltage that would develop between $u$ and $v$ when one unit of current is injected. This yields a proper metric $\Omega$ satisfying the triangle inequality (a fact that fails for shortest-path distance on multigraphs), and it exposes global connectivity: $\Omega(u, v) \le 1$ for any pair adjacent by a single edge, with equality holding *only* when that edge is a bridge (its removal disconnects the graph). The metric has a random-walk interpretation via the Chandra-Raghavan-Ruzzo-Smolensky commute-time formula $C(u, v) = 2m \cdot \Omega(u, v)$, where $m = |E|$; that identity makes $\Omega$ a natural fit for algorithms that reason about mixing times. Compute cost is $O(n^3)$ through the Laplacian pseudoinverse $L^+$. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Between two directly connected nodes in a simple graph, the resistance distance is exactly 1.0, matching a single 1-ohm resistor: ::: {#680251a0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph() g.add_full_graph(2) # Returns 1.0 g.get_resistance_distance(1, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1.0 ``` ::: ::: On a path, resistors are effectively in series, so resistance distance grows linearly with the number of edges between two nodes: ::: {#b651a4cd .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = ec.Graph() path.add_path_graph(4) # 1-2-3-4 # Returns (1.0, 2.0, 3.0): resistance grows with the number of edges between nodes ( path.get_resistance_distance(1, 2), path.get_resistance_distance(1, 3), path.get_resistance_distance(1, 4), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1.0000000000000004, 2.000000000000001, 3.000000000000001) ``` ::: ::: A cycle offers two parallel paths between any pair of nodes, which lowers the effective resistance compared to a single path of the same length: ::: {#9cb517e3 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} cycle = ec.Graph() cycle.add_cycle_graph(4) # 1-2-3-4-1 # Returns 0.75: parallel paths of length 1 and 3 combine to less than either alone cycle.get_resistance_distance(1, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0.7499999999999996 ``` ::: :::
